Arylalkylation of 1,3-Enynes to Access Chiral Tetrasubstituted
Allenes
Jinze Du, Anyao Liu, Wen Zhang, Shan Luo, Hequan Yao,* and Yuli He*

ABSTRACT: The enantio- and regioselective reductive 1,4-arylalkylation of 1,3-enynes has been successfully accomplished using a
nickel catalyst in conjunction with a chiral bulk bis-oxazoline ligand. This method facilitates the efficient synthesis of a wide variety of
structurally diverse, enantioenriched tetrasubstituted allenes, which are key structural motifs in numerous pharmacologically active
compounds and natural products. The reaction proceeds under mild conditions and is operationally straightforward. Mechanistic
investigations indicate that the reaction follows a radical pathway.
KEYWORDS: nickel catalysis, radical relay, chiral tetrasubstituted allenes, asymmetric reductive coupling, 1,4-arylalkylation
■
INTRODUCTION
In recent years, nickel catalysis has become pivotal in diverse
transformations due to its ability to accommodate various
oxidation states and engage in both one- and two-electron
pathways.
1
This versatility has revolutionized cross-coupling
and reductive coupling reactions,
2
addressing challenges posed
by other transition metals in the d
10
series. With the strategic
selection of chiral ligands, nickel catalysis has enabled extensive
exploration of enantioselective 1,2-difunctionalization of
unsaturated hydrocarbons, facilitating the synthesis of valuable
chiral molecules.
3
This is particularly significant given the
pivotal role of enantioenriched sp
3
-hybridized carbon centers
in organic synthesis (Figure 1, left).
4
However, the
enantioselective 1,4-difunctionalization of 1,3-enynes to access
sp
2
-hybridized carbon centers through nickel catalysis remains
an untapped area of research (Figure 1, right).
5
1,3-Enynes, which feature conjugated double and triple
bonds, are versatile synthons in organic synthesis. Recently, the
radical-based 1,4-functionalization of 1,3-enynes, utilizing
allenyl or propargylic radicals, has emerged as an area of
significant research interest, demonstrating potential for novel
synthesis pathways and product diversification.
6
Despite this
interest, achieving asymmetric 1,4-functionalization through
radical pathways remains a formidable challenge,
7
yet it
remains crucial due to its role in synthesizing chiral allenes,
8
which are not only critical structural elements in natural
products and bioactive molecules but also serve as dynamic
synthons and catalysts, significantly enhancing the scope of
organic synthesis (Figure 2a).
9
For instance, Bao
7a
and Liu
7b
independently described a Cu-catalyzed enantioselective
process for synthesizing chiral allenes via the radical 1,4-
dicarbylation of 1,3-enynes (Figure 2b up). Subsequently, the
Wang group

trisubstituted chiral α-allenols with notable enantio- and
diastereoselectivities, facilitated by a propargylic radical
intermediate (Figure 2b down). These radical-driven processes
operate under mild conditions and enable the formation of
densely functionalized complexes through a multicomponent
approach, thus broadening the scope for modifying 1,3-enynes.
The continued exploration of new radical-involved reaction
mechanisms is anticipated to enhance the efficient synthesis of
valuable chiral allenes, suggesting a promising direction for
future research on organic synthesis.
In response to this challenge, we investigated the feasibility
of a nickel-catalyzed 1,4-dicarbylation of 1,3-enynes to facilitate
multicomponent cross-electrophile couplings for the synthesis
of enantioenriched tetrasubstituted allenes. Herein, we report
the successful development of a tandem nickel-catalyzed
enantioselective C(sp
3

3

2

2

coupling reaction between aryl bromides, unactivated alkyl
halides, and enyne congeners (Figure 2c). This protocol,
characterized by its simplicity and broad substrate scope, offers
a complementary approach for preparing chiral tetrasubstituted
allenes from simple precursors with precise control over
selectivity at both alkene and allene double bond positions.
■

Our investigations commenced with an examination of the
reaction involving methyl 4-bromobenzoate (1a) with oct-1-
en-3-yn-2-ylbenzene (1a) and 2-iodo-2-methylpropane (3a).
After rigorous experimentation, we discovered that employing
a combination of NiCl

82% isolated yield with a single regioisomer and excellent
enantioselectivity (92% ee) (Table 1, entry 1). The choice of
ligands significantly influenced the reaction outcome. Notably,
other ligands (L4*−L6*), known for their efficacy in
asymmetric reductive difunctionalization of alkenes and
cross-couplings,

yield further improvements in the results.

the remarkable versatility of our protocol across a diverse array
of aryl bromides, alkyl iodides, and 1,3-enyne substrates.
Notably, regardless of whether electron-deficient or electron-
rich bromoarenes were utilized as coupling partners,
consistently good yields and excellent ee values were achieved.
An extensive range of functional groups, encompassing esters
(4a), ketones (4b), aldehydes (4c), nitriles (4e, 4k),
sulfonamides (4f), and sulfur ethers (4r), were adeptly
accommodated within the reaction framework. Importantly,
the compatibility of our methodology with functionalities
conducive to Ni-catalyzed transformations, such as aryl
fluorides (4j, 4k, 4o, 4q), aryl chlorides (4n, 4s), and aryl
triflates (4h), was demonstrated, ensuring avenues for further
diversification through conventional cross-coupling method-
ologies remained open.
1
Heterocyclic motifs, including
pyridines (4n−4p) and pyrimidines (4q−4r), emerged as
effective coupling partners, further broadening the synthetic
utility of our approach. Table 2B showcases the successful
application of our methodology to a plethora of 1,3-enynes
bearing both aromatic and aliphatic termini. Particularly
noteworthy was the observation that enynes featuring
electron-donating substituents on the arene moiety displayed
enhanced enantioselectivity profiles (5a, 5g vs 5b−5f, 5h).
Crucially, the X-ray crystallographic analysis of product 5a
provided unambiguous evidence regarding the stereochemical
outcome, elucidating the configuration of the difunctionalized
arene with an R-configuration allene. Furthermore, enynes
bearing ortho-substituted arenes (5c) were smoothly accom-
modated within the reaction manifold. In terms of 1,3-enynes
possessing substituents at the 4-position, those featuring benzyl
or purely aliphatic functional groups (5j−5k) were afforded in
good yields with exemplary enantioselectivity. Notably, diverse
functionalities, such as cyclopropyl (5k), chloride (5l), or silyl
(5m) moieties, positioned at various distances from the allenyl
radicals, were well-tolerated, furnishing chiral allenes with up
to 96% ee. Our reaction exhibited consistent applicability
across various unactivated alkyl iodides bearing different
substituents (Table 2C). Notably, tertiary (6a−6i), secondary
(6j−6o) as well as primary alkyl iodides (6p) displayed similar
outcomes, affirming the robustness of our approach. The

6n), nitriles (6e), thiophene (6f), and indole (6g), among
others. Nonetheless, the stereochemical outcome was less

The synthetic utility of our protocol is further highlighted in
Scheme 1a. As shown, a 5 mmol scale enantioselective
reductive 1,4-arylalkylation was performed successfully. Our
investigation proceeded to elucidate the reaction mechanism
through a series of control experiments. Introduction of the
radical scavenger TEMPO (2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidinooxy)
into the reaction mixture under the standard conditions
resulted in a diminished yield. This reduction was accom-
panied by the conspicuous formation of radical-trapped
products, confirmed by high-resolution mass spectrometry
(refer to 6.1 in the Supporting Information) (Scheme 1b). To
interrogate the reaction intermediates, a radical clock experi-
ment was conducted using substrate 2n. The ensuing reaction
furnished the ring-opening product 5n in 32% yield, providing
compelling evidence for the involvement of alkyl radicals
(Scheme 1c). Moreover, upon subjecting the stereospecific
substrate 3q to standard conditions, the resulting chiral allene
6q was formed in a racemic manner (1:1 dr), thereby
suggesting that the generation of secondary alkyl radical
species induced racemization. In the presence of MeOH (1.0
equiv), the reaction yielded the desired product 4a alongside
the protonated byproduct 7a (Scheme 1e). Notably, this
outcome suggests the occurrence of a propargyl or allenyl
radical intermediate prior to recombination with ArNi(II)Br.
The reaction exhibits first-order dependence on nickel, ligand,
and aryl bromide, underscoring their critical roles in the
process. In contrast, the zero-order dependence on alkene,
alkyl iodide, zinc, and sodium iodide indicates that these
components do not substantially affect the reaction rate.
Consequently, it is likely that the oxidative addition of aryl
bromide is the rate-determining step (Scheme 1f). Addition-

In light of these mechanistic insights and prior research, a
proposed catalytic cycle is outlined in Figure 3. We postulated
that a suitable L*Ni(0) catalyst could facilitate oxidative
addition at the Ar−Br site, leading to the formation of the
ArNi(II)Br II intermediate. Simultaneously, Ni(I) species
generated in the reaction mixture could activate the alkyl
iodide,
12
generating an alkyl radical VI which then adds onto
the C = C bond to form the propargyl radical VII and allenyl
radical III. Subsequently, ArNi(II)Br II can react with
intermediate III to yield pivotal Ni(III) species IV. Reductive
elimination of IV would furnish the desired difunctionalized
framework (4) along with a Ni(I) intermediate (V) that would
ultimately regenerate the catalytic L*Ni(0) species upon
single-electron transfer (SET) with an alkyl halide (3a) and Zn
as the terminal reductant.
■
CONCLUSIONS
In summary, we have developed a de novo platform that
facilitates the synthesis of 1,4-difunctionalized allenes with
outstanding enantioselectivities, catalyzed by nickel utilizing a
novel chiral bulk bis-oxazoline ligand. This methodology
stands out for its broad substrate applicability and mild
reaction conditions, thereby providing a complementary
approach for achieving enantioselective reductive nickel-
catalyzed multicomponent difunctionalization of alkenes.
Preliminary mechanistic investigations indicated the involve-
ment of a radical tandem process in the reaction. Ongoing
efforts are focused on expanding the scope of asymmetric
cross-electrophile 1,n-difunctionalization of alkenes, while
simultaneously progressing toward a deeper understanding of
the stereoselectivity mechanisms through DFT studies.
